paragraphs: Across the Dorset Council area you can foster with the council's own service or with one of the independent agencies listed above. The council says it wants to hear from people from all walks of life and encourages people not to rule themselves out before they have asked.

Dorset's approach is to keep children close to their own schools, friends and communities, and it says it offers its own approved carers a child first, before looking elsewhere. In its view that means people who foster with the council are more likely to be caring for a child sooner than through an independent agency, though it is worth asking every service you speak to how quickly it typically places children with new carers.

Support listed by the council includes a fostering social worker alongside the child's own social worker, a duty worker and an out-of-hours service, input from health staff, education staff and specialist psychologists, a youth service for children in care, regular local support groups, the Dorset Foster Carers Forum, free FosterTalk membership, the Fosterline counselling helpline, social events, an awards evening and support for carers' own children. New carers have an induction and work through the national training standards over their first 12 to 18 months, followed by a free programme of further learning.

Dorset is also one of the 14 councils in Fostering South West, a regional hub launched in April 2024, hosted by Wiltshire Council and funded by the Department for Education, which acts as a single first point of contact for anyone thinking about fostering with a council in the region. Talk to the council and two or three of the services above before deciding, and see the Somerset, Wiltshire, Devon and Hampshire pages if you live near the county's edge.

sources.title: Local council fostering partnership launched in the South West of England (Dorset Council, 4 November 2024)
